text: PEAK WATER.

label: text
text: GOVERNMENT STATEMENT BROADCAST

label: text
text:
MINIMUM CONSUMPTION.
Higher Levels Completely Isolated.

label: text
text: Publicity is now being resorted to by a Government office.

label: text
text:
This is hardly the time to bring in such a matter across the public.
"will recall the fact that the "China Mail" has all along advocated a department of information.

label: text
text: Apparently, the value of "judicious propaganda has been reknitted as the P.W.D. is broadcasting a notice on the water supply to the higher levels.

label: text
text: The main facts were given in yesterday's "China Mail." The notice reads:

label: paragraph_title
text: FACITS & FIGURES

label: text
text: The Peak, Conduit Road and Robinson Road districts are entirely supplied from the Pokfulam Road pumping station with water.

label: text
text: Water is pumped to the 750 ft. tank situated close to Hattom Road and the water gravitates from this tank, which when full holds 388,000 gallons to Conduit Road and May Road as far as the May Road Peak Tram station; and Robinson Road as far as Peak Road (Seth's Corner).

label: text
text: The Peak supply is pumped to the Peak reservoir, which holds when full 395,000 gallons, and is situated just below the Peak flagstaff. Water from the Peak reservoir, gravitates all over the Peak district west and south of Findlay Path and Plantation Road.

label: text
text: Water also gravitates from the Peak reservoir at night to Mount Gough service reservoir, which holds when full 211,000 gallons, and is situated on the summit of Mt. Gough above "Tanderagee." Mt. Gough service reservoir serves all the Peak district east and north of Findlay Path and Plantation Road to Wanchai Gap and Mt. Cameron.

label: text
text: Pokfulam Road pumping station contains three engines. Nos. 1, 2 and 3, the combined capacity of Nos. 1 and 2 being equal to the capacity of No. 3. These three pumps give the only supply to the Peak and high level districts.

label: text
text: On Monday a large boulder weighing between $2,000 and $3,000 tons fell from the hillside and completely demolished the eastern end of the pumping station, carrying away the Eliot approach road and seven pumping and supply mains and completely wrecking No. 3 engine.

label: text
text: No. 2 engine at the time of the accident was under overhaul and therefore dismantled, the dismantled portion being in the eastern half of the pumping station which is now under hundreds of tons of rock.

label: text
text: The only pump therefore left intact is the No. 1, or one quarter of the capacity of the original pumping station, and this pump cannot be operated until one of the pumping mains has been repaired. The whole of the higher levels is therefore completely isolated and is meantime entirely dependent on the water left in the Peak reservoir, Mt. Gough reservoir and 750 ft. tank—a rapidly dwindling quantity.

label: text
text: Work is at present being concentrated on the repair of one high level pumping main and it is hoped to get this through by Sunday or Monday when it will be possible to pump a small supply.

label: text
text: Work in the second place is being concentrated on the repair of No. 2 engine, but as both new forgings and castings are necessary it may be a month before this can be completed.

label: text
text: It is impossible so far to say how much, if any, of the No. 3 engine can be saved...but in any case it will be many months before a full supply can be resumed in the Peak and high level distriets.

label: text
text: This explanation is issued so that consumers may realise the real state of affairs and take the necessary steps to reduce to a minimum the consumption of water from the mains.

label: text
text: Water from nullahs should meantime be collected for washing and flushing purposes till further notice.

label: text
text: Drinking water should be boiled.

text: TWO SHIPS ASHORE.

label: doc_title
text: INTENSE GALE MISSES BY 40 MILES.

label: text
text: Typhoon Stops All Business & Law Courts.

label: text
text: A very intense typhoon—the second to pass Hongkong this season — caused considerable havoc this morning.

label: text
text: Two sea-going steamers have already been blown aground. At mid-day, a river steamboat was drifting helplessly in another part of the harbour, assistance not being possible in the furious weather.

label: text
text: Although the "blow" was not felt very much in the city, business and the Law Courts and all business centres were at a standstill.

label: text
text: According to one expert, the “glass” has shown a record:

label: text
text: No calamity of importance had been reported by noon, on shore.

label: text
text:
Expected yesterday to be making a bee-line for Hongkong, this typhoon showed practically no deviation at all and the centre missed us by 40 miles. It was so intense that—in the opinion of a Royal Naval officer—we would have been blown to bits if it had struck us with full force.
Government "red tape" precludes the "China Mail" from obtaining details as to squall velocity "barometer readings". A private instrument, on sea-level; "Hongkong" side, recorded 29.18 early this morning, before the change in signals: Towards 1 p.m., the reading was 29.19 and steady. Our informant thinks this is a record but is open to correction.

label: text
text:
Ships in Distress.
The ships in distress are the s.s. "Pawnee," the s.s. "Confucius," and the steamboat "Ting On."
The "Pawnee" has two funnels and is familiar to Stonecutters bathers having lain up for months, at anchor, outside Yaumati Bay, between Stonecutters and the breakwater. The "Seistan" was another idle vessel in that locality but she went out to a harbour buoy and was safe.

label: paragraph_title
text: Drifted Ashore

label: text
text: Unable to stay against the wind, the "Pawnee" drifted westwards, by Stonecutters until she heared Kapsuimun, the passage from Hongkong to Macao and Canton. On one side was Chung Hue Island, on which is the Royal Artillery datum (a patch of cliff painted white) and Kap Sing lighthouse. The "Pawnee" was ultimately driven ashore on Chung Hue. Owing to the weather prevailing assistance had not been despatched at the time of writing nor is it known if the ship is in immediate danger of sinking, or breaking up.

label: text
text:
The s.s. "China Arrow" reported sighting a vessel ashore at Chung. Hue. Then the Government rescue tug "Kau Sing," which had been patrolling the harbour since the storm began, sent back another message.
Mr. C. J. Thompson, senior boarding officer of the Harbour Office, is in command, and he is in constant wireless communication with Lt.-Com. G. F. Hole, R.N. (Harbour Master).

label: text
text: The Kau Sing" identified the "Pawnee." But the tug was in dire distress herself. She was behind Stonecutters, two anchors down and actually steaming ahead to prevent her dragging anchors and being carried away by the elements.

label: text
text: Readers can. best image for themselves the state of the"weather" when it is remembered that the "Kau Sing," although of single screw, was in such a position—and she was built for typhoon.rescue.

label: text
text:
“Confucius” Ashore.
That clumsy looking vessel, the “Confucius” has gone aground in Kowloon Bay, off the China Light and Power Co.'s premises at Hunghom.

label: text
text: The “Confucius” was formerly a “Lake” boat on the U.S. Shipping Board feeder service and was sold to Chinese interests. She has been unemployed for some time and was anchored in Kowloon Bay to take refuge from the typhoon. Her fate is not

label: text
text: The river boat adrift is the "Ting On." which is 180 feet long. She had gone to Kwong Tuck Cheong's shipyard for repairs and was reported to be dragging her anchors in Kowloon Bay.

label: text
text: Until the typhoon abates, full details will not be available.

label: text
text: That there has been other damage is evident from the fact that a Government buoy was cut adrift. In the morning this mooring was noticed to be off Jardine's wharf, West Point praya. The bigger vessels which were at harbour buoys, or those which took up similar positions after yesterday's warning, are all reported to be safe.

label: text
text: Thanks to the courtesy of the Harbour Master, the “China Mail” has been able to reconstruct the path of the typhoon from the time it was first “spotted,” out in the Pacific.

label: text
text: This typhoon came along, passing between Luzon and Formosa, to the south of Pratas and Hongkong. In 66 hours, it travelled 900 miles. That is, it moved westwards (or W.N.W.) at a rate of about 13½ miles an hour. The maximum squall velocity (i.e., the strength of the wind revolving in the cyclone) can only be obtained from the Observatory, which is now inaccessible.

label: text
text: Of the supposedly abnormal air pressure, mention has already been made.

label: text
text: With the facts at hand, and the information that the typhoon was very intense—radius unknown—Hongkongites can still be thankful that they did not get the worse.

label: text
text:
Consulting expert opinion this morning. the “China Mail” was informed that if the typhoon maintained its course, it should strike the coast to the west of Hongkong; but, and here the speaker preferred to reserve his pronouncement, it may still curve in any direction so that all danger to the Colony is not entirely passed.
The previous typhoon followed a route somewhat to the south of the present one but took a right-angle turn towards Swatow. On nearing the coast, it curved again, outwards, round Swatow and went inland to cause Hongkong's deluge. This movement is considered phenomenal.

label: text
text:
The signals explain how the typhoon was anticipated here.
At 12:10 p.m. yesterday, No. 1 local signal was hoisted, (a red cone pointing upwards) meaning that a typhoon existed which may cause a gale in Hongkong within 24 hours.

label: text
text: At 4.20 p.m., there appeared the black-cone-pointing-upwards-(No.2) which meant: gale expected from the North (N.W. to N.E.)

label: text
text: At 6:30 a.m. to day; No. 6 went up. This is "the black double cone which means: Gale expected to increase. By this time the glass had fallen and it was fairly certain that the typhoon was coming here. As a matter of fact, the first signs of a blow were noticed about 3 a.m.

label: text
text:
By 7.45 a.m., No. 4 signal (a black drum) had superseded the others, meaning: gale expected from the East (N.E. to S.E.)—showing that danger was now expected from another direction.
About 10 a.m., a message came through thus: The typhoon is passing to a few miles South of Gap Rock (which is about 35 miles to the south of Hongkong), in a westerly direction; no great increase of wind is anticipated at Hongkong.

label: paragraph_title
text: "Empress" Delayed.

label: text
text: The R. M. S. "Empress of Russia" which was scheduled to leave at noon today, for Vancouver via ports, will not sail until the weather clears up. The liner, which was formerly alongside the dock in Kowloon, has now gone to buoy in midstream. Passengers and all concerned will be notified six hours before the liner's departure.

label: text
text: Mails from Home (letters and papers, London, June 24, and parcels) June 17) were due by the P. and O. steamer. "Macedonia," the vessel being scheduled to arrive at 6 a.m. to day. When inquiries were made at noon, it was ascertained that the vessel was outside Lyemeum Pass, waiting for better weather to make port.

label: text
text: The s.s. "President Wilson" arrived last night and anchored in Dowloon Bay. Mails from the U.S.A., Honolulu, Japan and Shanghai are still aboard.

label: paragraph_title
text: Other Ships

label: text
text: The S.S. "Talmok," also of the same line, is outside Kowloon Bay, and cannot possibly make her way in, it being impossible for the pilot to go on board.

label: text
text: All the vessels of the Indo-China Steam Navigation have taken refuge at Kowloon Bay, and are tied to typhoon "buoys, sailings being postponed until more favourable conditions." The S.S. "Yatshing" which was scheduled to leave yesterday for Shanghai, has been postponed until this afternoon, but has been unable to leave up to the present.

label: text
text: The Glenn Line, agents for the S.S. "Carnarvonshire" report that due to the typhoon, the "Carnavonshire" has not arrived in port and that they have not received any message from its skipper. The "Carnarvonshire" was scheduled to leave this afternoon for London.

text: At the moment of writing no official communique has reached the “China Mail” regarding the conference, at Canton, to negotiate for a settlement of the boycott.

text: According to arrangement, the two delegations resumed meeting at the Foreign Office yesterday morning, when the proceedings are stated to have lasted twenty minutes.

label: text
text: The typhoon which passed Hongkong on Saturday and struck the coast south of Swatow did not cause any damage amongst shipping so far as can be ascertained from reports received at the Harbour Office. The majority report having experienced "heavy swell, squalls, moderate winds," etc.

label: text
text: No further news is available with regard to the s.s. "Nankai Maru," owned by the Kaium Kabushiki Kaisha of Tarumi, which sent out a distress signal received by local stations when the ship was approximately 400 miles S.E. of Hongkong and 100 miles east of the northern coast of Luzon.

label: paragraph_title
text: LOCAL ITEMS.

label: text
text:
Although Hongkong may count itself fortunate in that it has escaped the main force of the typhoon, the high wind and rain that has fallen to our portion as its "backwash" has undone much of the work of repair that was in hand in connection with the clearances of roads. The extent of this damage it is impossible to state at the moment owing to the difficulty of survey work.
Also, it may be added, it is too soon to assume that Hongkong is definitely clear of the typhoon but the only chance of our being involved in its train is in the case of a very definite turn.

label: paragraph_title
text: Early Ferries.

label: text
text: Although during the period in which the No. 6 signal was up the red flag (signifying that ferries might stop at any minute) was visible at the "Star" ferry wharf the ferries continued running until shortly after 9 a.m. although considerable difficulty was experienced in effecting a landing. One ferry, in fact, after bringing passengers across the harbour from Kowloon had to turn back after making unavailing efforts to get near enough the wharf to render safe the lowering of the gangway.

label: text
text:
The last ferry to discharge passengers on the Hongkong side successfully accomplished the feat at 9.10 but without lowering the gangway. The pier head was used as a fulcrum for bringing the boat alongside and it was then possible for passengers to jump ashore. The very heavy seas running caused the boats to roll a great deal in the course of the passage across and difficulty was experienced in making the wharf. The set of the current took several of the boats in the direction of Queen's pier but they were all able to make up leeway.
The ferries re-commenced running shortly after 1 p.m.

label: text
text: The waves broke over the Prayer occasionally in the central districts but this was more noticeable in the West Point area where accumulations of debris have been flung ashore. A human body afloat was plainly visible near the Pottinger wharf.
